vocab.gloss: of; ~'s (possessive particle); (used after an attribute); (used to form a nominal expression)

grammar.title: Possessive 的 — and when Taiwanese speakers drop it
grammar.pattern: X + 的 + 名詞;家人時 的 可以不說:我(的)媽媽
grammar.explanation: 的 links an owner to what is owned: 老闆的女兒 (the boss's daughter), 我的手機 (my phone). With family members and other very close relations, everyday Taiwan speech usually drops 的: 我爸爸, 我媽媽, 我兒子 sound more natural than 我的爸爸. When 的 ends the sentence, the noun is understood: 傘是誰的? = Whose umbrella is it?
grammar.contrast: 我媽媽 vs 我的手機. What decides it is the noun: family words (爸爸/媽媽/兒子/女兒) and things you belong to (我家, 我學校) let you drop 的; ordinary objects keep it. You can never drop 的 in 老闆的兒子 either — dropping works mainly after 我/你.
grammar.common_error: Two habits: saying 我的爸爸 every single time, which sounds stiff and translated; and dropping the final 的 in questions or answers, e.g. saying 傘是誰? or 腳踏車是我 instead of 傘是誰的? / 腳踏車是我的.

examples.gloss: The boss's daughter is really pretty.

grammar.title: 家有誰?asking who is in someone's family
grammar.pattern: 你家有誰? / 我家有 + 家人
grammar.explanation: To ask about family members, Taiwanese speakers say 你家有誰?The answer simply lists people with 有: 我家有爸爸、媽媽。誰 works as both question word and normal noun position, so the word order never changes.
grammar.contrast: 你家有誰? asks which people; 你家有什麼? asks about things. Use 誰 only for people.
grammar.common_error: Learners move 誰 to the front like English 'who', saying 誰你家有?The question word stays in the object slot: 你家有誰?

passage.title: 我家的人
passage.hanzi: 我家有爸爸、媽媽,我是家中的兒子。爸爸是老師,天天騎腳踏車上班。媽媽開一家早餐店,客人好喜歡媽媽的紅茶。週末爸爸、媽媽帶我搭捷運逛書店。晚上一家人一起吃飯,好高興。
passage.gloss: My family has my dad, my mom, and me — I'm the son of the house. My dad is a teacher and rides his bike to work every day. My mom runs a breakfast shop, and the customers really love her black tea. On weekends my parents take me on the MRT to browse bookstores. In the evening the whole family eats together, and it's wonderful.

grammar.title: A 和 B 都… (A and B both …)
grammar.pattern: A + 和 + B + 都 + verb / adjective
grammar.explanation: 和 (Taiwan pronunciation hàn) joins two nouns or pronouns into one subject: 他和她, 我和朋友. When that joint subject does the same thing, add 都 right before the verb or adjective to say 'both / all'. 都 never goes at the front of the sentence and never goes after the verb: 我和他都有悠遊卡, not 都我和他有悠遊卡.
grammar.contrast: 和 vs. just listing two clauses: 和 links nouns only. For two actions you do NOT use 和 — you say them as two clauses: 我吃飯，看書 (I eat and read), never 我吃飯和看書. If the two people do different things, drop 都: 他吃麵，她吃飯。
grammar.common_error: Learners copy English 'both … and' and put 都 before the subject, or leave 都 out completely. In Chinese the 'both' word 都 must sit after the subject and directly before the verb, and it is normally required once you say 'A 和 B'.

examples.pinyin: Tā hàn tā dōu shì xuéshēng.
examples.gloss: He and she are both students.

passage.title: 我的同學小文
passage.hanzi: 小文是我的同學。她家附近有一家早餐店，老闆和他的兒子都認識她。今天早上，我們一起騎腳踏車上學，天氣晴，風不大。中午我和她都吃便當，下午一起走路逛書店。她說明天她媽媽會帶我們搭捷運。
passage.gloss: Xiaowen is my classmate. There's a breakfast shop near her house, and both the owner and his son know her. This morning we rode our bikes to school together; the weather was clear and there wasn't much wind. At noon she and I both had bento boxes, and in the afternoon we walked around a bookstore together. She said that tomorrow her mom will take us on the MRT.

grammar.title: Asking amounts: 幾 vs 多少
grammar.pattern: 幾 + 量詞 + (名詞)？ ／ 多少 + (名詞)？
grammar.explanation: 幾 asks about a small, countable number (usually under ten) and must be followed by a measure word: 幾歲、幾點、幾號、幾塊錢. 多少 asks about any amount, big or small, and normally goes straight in front of the noun: 多少錢、多少學生. When you ask a child's age you say 你幾歲？; for prices, which can be any number, Taiwanese people say 多少錢？
grammar.contrast: 幾塊錢 vs 多少錢: both ask a price, but 幾塊錢 already assumes the answer is only a few dollars, while 多少錢 is neutral and is what you actually say in a shop. The size of the expected number is what decides.
grammar.common_error: Learners drop the measure word after 幾 and say things like 幾錢 or 幾書. 幾 almost never touches the noun directly — put a measure word in between. The other frequent slip is asking an adult 你幾歲？, which sounds like you are talking to a small child.

examples.gloss: How old are you this year?

examples.pinyin: Zhè bēi zhēnzhū nǎichá duōshǎo qián?
examples.gloss: How much is this cup of bubble tea?
How many students are there in your class?

grammar.title: 太……了
grammar.explanation: 太 means 'too / excessively' and almost always takes 了 at the end: 太多了、太少了、太熱了. It can also be a compliment in fixed phrases like 太好了 ('great!').
grammar.contrast: 很 + adjective is simply 'very' and is neutral; 太……了 says the amount has gone past what you want. 他吃很少 just reports a fact; 他吃太少了 complains about it.
grammar.common_error: Saying 太多 or 太熱 with no 了 in a complete sentence. In everyday Taiwan speech the 了 is expected: 今天客人太多了。

examples.gloss: There are too many customers today.

examples.gloss: He ate far too little today.

passage.title: 我家的珍珠
passage.hanzi: 我家的貓叫珍珠，今年一歲多。朋友看他都說：「珍珠太小了，他幾歲了？」我說他還是小朋友。珍珠吃得很少，有時一天沒吃多少東西，我就帶他去看醫生。醫生說他沒事，不用吃藥。現在珍珠很愛吃飯，也喜歡坐在桌子上看外面的雨。
passage.gloss: My cat is called Zhenzhu (Pearl); she's a bit over one year old this year. Friends who see her all say, "Pearl is so tiny — how old is she?" I tell them she's still a kid. Pearl eats very little, and some days she hardly eats anything, so I take her to the vet. The vet says she's fine and doesn't need medicine. These days Pearl loves her food, and she also likes to sit on the table and watch the rain outside.
